cards.front: What's wrong with "Although the price is high, but the quality is good"?
cards.back: Double conjunction — English only needs ONE conjunction to show contrast. Correct: "Although the price is high, the quality is good." (This is your #1 most repeated grammar error.)

cards.front: Fix: "The satisfaction level does not fluctuate" vs the wrong version "the satisfaction level not fluctuate" — why is the second one wrong?
cards.back: English negation of a regular verb needs an auxiliary: S + do/does/did + not + V. "Not" can never sit directly before a normal verb (unlike Vietnamese "không").

cards.front: "The amount of percentage for both groups ___ (is/are) stable." Which is correct and why?
cards.back: "is" — the verb agrees with the HEAD NOUN ("amount", singular), not the noun inside the following prepositional phrase ("percentage"). This is a recurring trap in chart descriptions.

cards.front: Why must you write "the US" / "the UK" instead of just "US" / "UK" in formal writing?
cards.back: Country abbreviations/acronyms take a definite article: "the US", "the UK". Dropping "the" before these is one of your recurring article errors.

cards.front: Fix: "Overall, the chart shows that China dominants the retail market."
cards.back: "dominants" isn't a real word. Correct: "China dominates the retail market." Rule: 3rd-person singular subject + V(+s). "Dominant" is the adjective/noun form, "dominates" is the verb.

cards.front: Fix: "The very poor group... which steady decline from 5% to 2%."
cards.back: "steady" is an adjective but here it's modifying a verb ("decline") — you need the adverb "steadily". Rule: adjectives modify nouns, adverbs modify verbs. Correct: "...which steadily declines from 5% to 2%."

cards.front: Fix: "The scientist whom I interviewed him studies climate change."
cards.back: Remove "him" — it's a redundant pronoun. "Whom" already functions as the object of "interviewed", so you can't repeat the object with "him". Correct: "The scientist whom I interviewed studies climate change."

cards.front: What is a "comma splice" and why is it a grammar error?
cards.back: Joining two independent (full) clauses with only a comma, e.g. "Prices rose, sales fell." Fix by using a period, semicolon, or a conjunction (and/but/so): "Prices rose, so sales fell." This is a repeated error across your responses.

cards.front: Fix the spelling: "the cycle repeats it self every year."
cards.back: Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, itself, themselves) are always ONE word — never split. Correct: "the cycle repeats itself every year."

cards.front: Fix: "Finally the flower turns into a fruit to complete the a full cycle."
cards.back: Two errors: (1) missing comma after transition word "Finally,"; (2) "the a full cycle" has two articles stacked — only one article per noun phrase. Correct: "Finally, the flower turns into a fruit to complete a full cycle."

cards.front: When describing a chart/graph in PTE, should you use present or past tense, and why?
cards.back: Present simple — "the chart shows...", not "showed". The data represents a general/ongoing fact (like a snapshot of reality), similar to "Water boils at 100°C". Use past tense only for specific historical events (e.g., "In 2020, sales dropped by 10%").

cards.front: Fix: "The meeting room locates in the corner of the building."
cards.back: "Locate" is transitive and normally needs the passive form for stative location. Correct: "The meeting room is located in the corner." Same rule applies to "situate" (→ "is situated").

cards.front: Should "receive" be put in passive voice in English, the way Vietnamese "được nhận" implies passivity?
cards.back: No. "Receive" is already active-voice with the receiver as subject: "I received a gift." Only use passive if the THING RECEIVED becomes the subject: "A gift was received by me" (rare/unnatural). Don't translate "được" into an unnecessary passive.

cards.front: Fix: "Leisure activities take three times as much hours as eating and drinking."
cards.back: "Hours" is countable, so use "many" not "much": "as many hours as". (Also double-check your math against the actual chart data before choosing a multiplier like "three times".)

cards.front: In formal PTE writing, should you write numbers like "5" as digits or words?
cards.back: Numbers under 10 should be spelled out in formal writing: "five stages", not "5 stages". (Percentages and large statistics can stay as digits, e.g. "54.6%".)

cards.front: Can "followed by" be followed directly by a full clause (S + V)?
cards.back: No — "followed by" + NOUN PHRASE only, e.g. "planting, followed by watering." To connect two full clauses in sequence, use "and this was followed by", "then", or "after" instead. Important for Process Diagram descriptions.

cards.front: How should you format currency in writing: "3.99$" or "$3.99"?
cards.back: "$3.99" — the currency symbol goes BEFORE the number in English.

cards.front: Is "peoples" ever correct as a plural?
cards.back: "People" is already the plural of "person" (don't add -s for a group of individuals). "Peoples" is only correct when referring to multiple distinct ethnic/national groups, e.g. "the peoples of Southeast Asia."

cards.front: Should you use contractions like "it's", "don't" in PTE Writing responses?
cards.back: No — avoid contractions in formal/academic PTE Writing and Speaking. Always write full forms: "it is", "do not". Contractions signal an informal register, which examiners penalize.

cards.front: Fix: "That two reasons account for most decisions."
cards.back: Demonstrative must match plural noun: "Those two reasons account for most decisions." (that → singular, those → plural)

cards.front: Fix: "The very poor group taking fairly smaller proportion..."
cards.back: "taking" isn't a finite verb — a clause needs one. Also "fairly smaller" is a bad collocation; use "much/far smaller" with comparatives. Correct: "The very poor group takes up a much smaller proportion..."

cards.front: Which preposition is correct: "females engage ___ work" — "on" or "in"?
cards.back: "in" — "engage IN" is a fixed collocation. Learn fixed preposition pairs as whole chunks rather than translating word-by-word from Vietnamese.

cards.front: What structural element is most often missing at the start of a Describe Image / line-graph response?
cards.back: An OVERVIEW SENTENCE stating what the chart shows, what's being compared, and the time frame. Its absence costs content/structure points even if the rest of the description is accurate.

cards.front: Practical PTE rule: when is "whom" actually required instead of "who"?
cards.back: Only when it comes immediately after a preposition, e.g. "the professor TO WHOM I spoke". In most other cases "who" is acceptable and sounds more natural — if unsure, use "who".

cards.front: Can "whose" be used for things, not just people?
cards.back: Yes. "Whose" shows possession for both people and things: "the report whose findings shocked everyone" (= "its findings"). Many learners wrongly think it's people-only.

cards.front: Backshift rule: "The report indicates that sales ___ (rise/rose) last quarter." Which form, and why?
cards.back: "rose" (or "had risen" if it happened before another past event) — when a reporting clause uses "that", tense shifts back one level (present → past). This pattern is core for SWT reporting verbs (indicates, shows, reports + that-clause).

cards.front: What does "cited" mean, as in "reasons cited by customers"?
cards.back: Mentioned or referred to as a reason/source (e.g., in a survey). Don't confuse with homophones "site" (a location) or "sight" (vision/a view).

cards.front: Why does "considerable variation" take NO article, while "a variation of the recipe" DOES?
cards.back: "Variation" is uncountable when it refers to a general degree of difference (considerable variation = a lot of difference). It's countable when it means one specific variant/version of something (a variation of the recipe = one version).

cards.front: What's the correct idiom for the lowest point on a chart, contrasted with the highest? ("on the other side of the scale" is WRONG)
cards.back: "at the other end of the scale" — e.g., "By contrast, Canada sits at the other end of the scale, having produced only 80 films."

cards.front: What does a perfect participle clause like "...having produced only 80 films" add, compared to a simple -ing clause?
cards.back: It shows a COMPLETED action that happened before/leads to the main clause's situation — a more precise causal/temporal relationship ("having + V3"). Using this structure signals grammatical range, which PTE rewards.

cards.front: What's a more natural/academic phrase than "takes up" when describing a data share? E.g. "Price takes up 54.6%."
cards.back: "accounts for" — "Price accounts for 54.6% of the decision." "Takes up" is too casual for formal chart description.

cards.front: Fix: "China ranks at first in retail sales."
cards.back: "ranks first" — no preposition needed before an ordinal like "first/last" after "rank".

cards.front: How can you avoid repeating "total retail sales" three times in one response?
cards.back: Vary your vocabulary with synonyms: "share", "online retail spending", "the percentage". Repetition is penalized; range of vocabulary is rewarded.

cards.front: Name 4-5 strong "trend" verbs to use instead of flatly listing numbers in a chart description.
cards.back: rise, climb, increase, grow, edge up (upward); fall, decline, drop, plunge (downward). These sound more natural and analytical than just stating percentages.

cards.front: What are the format/length constraints for Summarize Written Text (SWT)?
cards.back: ONE single sentence, 5–75 words, that captures the main idea + key supporting point. It's a compression skill, not a creativity skill.

cards.front: What is the best single sentence pattern/template for SWT?
cards.back: "Although/While + [supporting detail], + [main idea] + because/as + [reason]." This compresses a whole paragraph into one grammatically complex sentence — the single most useful SWT structure.

cards.front: What's the recommended length and structure for the PTE Essay task?
cards.back: 200-300 words: a clear position, 2-3 supporting paragraphs, and a conclusion.

cards.front: What is the recommended 4-part structure for Describe Image (process/cycle diagrams)?
cards.back: 1) Overview, 2) Stage-by-stage detail, 3) Cycle/Result (or trend insight for graphs), 4) Conclusion. Close with a sentence restating the cycle/topic keywords, which helps the AI scorer recognize completeness.

cards.front: What is the recommended 4-part structure for Describe Image (floor plan / spatial diagrams)?
cards.back: 1) Overview, 2) Entrance/Starting point, 3) Spatial movement (using location prepositions & movement verbs), 4) Conclusion.

cards.front: For a 60+ PTE target, what matters more: grammar accuracy or vocabulary complexity?
cards.back: Grammar accuracy. One clean, error-free sentence scores better than one ambitious sentence with a mistake. Don't reach for words/structures you're not sure how to use correctly.

cards.front: What's the recommended time budget for SWT and Essay?
cards.back: SWT: ~10 minutes. Essay: ~20 minutes. Many learners lose points not from grammar but from running out of time to write a proper conclusion.

cards.front: What's the recommended process for reviewing feedback after each practice submission?
cards.back: 1) Fix only the top 1-2 flagged issues first, not everything at once. 2) Physically retype the corrected sentences yourself. 3) Keep a running list of repeated mistakes. 4) Do a before/after comparison every 5-10 responses.

cards.front: Besides Summarize Written Text and Write Essay, which other task types secretly also feed into your PTE Writing score?
cards.back: Summarize Spoken Text and Write from Dictation — both are listed under "Listening" but are integrated tasks that also contribute to your Writing score. Don't neglect them when trying to raise Writing.

cards.front: Quick self-check habit for articles: what question should you ask before every singular countable noun?
cards.back: "Is this a singular countable noun?" → If yes, it needs an article (a/an/the). This habit fixes your recurring pattern of dropping articles (e.g., "wide range" → "a wide range").

cards.front: Quick self-check habit for subject-verb agreement: what should you check before submitting any sentence?
cards.back: Does the subject end in "-s" (plural) or not (singular)? Then make sure the verb form matches — this is your single most repeated error type across chart descriptions.
